breaking-down-the-work:
- Break the deliverable into product-first nouns (components, docs, subsystems), never action verbs; verbs only appear in a labeled activity layer beneath a work package.
- Enforce the 100% rule: children must cover exactly the parent's scope, no gaps or invented work; write any deferred scope as an explicit gap line.
- Enforce no overlaps/one home per piece: fix overlaps by re-cutting boundaries or lifting shared work into one common piece, never by duplicating.
- Number pieces with outline traceability and write a dictionary entry (scope, in/out, deliverable, interfaces, acceptance, size, owner, dependencies) for every piece; stop breaking down once a leaf is ownable/estimable/verifiable.
- Refuse to proceed without a single named top deliverable, refuse to produce schedules/cost estimates/compliance claims, and escalate to the owner when children can't sum without overlap.
briefing-an-agent:
- Build a context pack stating role, decision question, goal (with success signs/non-goals), affected files, current phase, and evidence required, using only what's needed for the next decision.
- State the agent's authority: allowed files/commands/tools, forbidden actions, do-not-touch targets, approval gates, and stop conditions—power must not exceed brief clarity.
- Include last completed action, changed conditions, critical next action, and likely mistake to guard against.
- Link back to the change record and mode rules; don't paste full source lineage or whole repo/standards.
- Stop or escalate if requested actions exceed stated power, or if credentials, production data, network effects, or release authority appear; use handing-off-work instead when transferring ownership of open work.
checking-legal-and-safety-wording:
- Keep "you may use it" (MIT permission) strictly separate from "it is proven fit"; never let public text imply the repo grants formal verification, compliance, certification, safety, security, or regulated-use fitness.
- Check changed public text (README, docs, templates, skills, commands, examples, release notes) against LICENSE, DISCLAIMER.md, SECURITY.md, and compliance-boundaries.md.
- Add "this does not create..." disclaimer wording near onboarding, templates, commands, and CLI help; replace assurance-sounding words with evidence-tied wording.
- Scan for banned claim phrases, ensuring they appear only in negative/disclaimer sentences, and confirm `python tools/ng.py doctor .` passes.
- Block/rework any overreaching claim before release; refuse and escalate requests for legal advice or regulated-use approval to a qualified professional.
checking-release-readiness:
- Before approving a release, verify baseline/artifacts, confirm evidence (not confidence) via actor/context/mechanism/authority/resource coupling review, check for scope/goal drift, confirm rollback, and confirm monitoring plans.
- Record one verdict—ship, block, defer, or ship-with-named-risk—naming the owner and authority coupling; for trust-bearing/irreversible work, block if coupling isn't explicitly accepted.
- For real-world actions, separately record apply-clearance (cleared/hold/lapsed) checking approvals, freeze window, unchanged external state, and rollback readiness; never treat a ship verdict as standing authorization.
- Reject rationalizations like "green CI means ship," "the agent's write-up says it's ready," or "the gap is probably fine"; block if rollback is impossible, monitoring is missing, or decisions rest only on the actor's own summary.
- Name the abort trigger, handoff need, and OPEX/new-baseline triggers; output an updated ship.md with decision, rationale, leftover risks, rollback, and monitoring notes.
checking-source-claims:
- Verify every cited source is public and listed in source-map.md; else mark "public URL needed" or downgrade to "supporting context."
- Reword all references as influence, idea lineage, or workflow inspiration—never as compliance, certification, approval, or formal assurance.
- Remove/negate any "compliant," "approved," "certified," or "formal" wording outside disclaimers.
- Update source-map.md and source-to-concept-crosswalk.md rows to match narrowed wording.
- Refuse to cite non-public, proprietary, or unverified sources as direct lineage; escalate if wording affects regulated, customer, or investor trust.
checking-what-a-change-affects:
- Before shipping any controlled change, screen every artifact it could leave stale: docs, tests, checkers, skills, commands, templates, prompts, releases, saved versions, and runtime blast radius (schema/state migration, API consumers, backward-compatibility, rollback-of-state).
- For each affected item, assign one action—update, leave alone, defer, or block—with linked evidence, an owner, and a re-check trigger; record this in `change-impact.md`.
- Never quietly accept a stale doc, test, checker, template, skill, command, or runtime contract; carry blockers or accepted gaps into `ship.md`.
- Escalate or stop if the change touches outside trust, security, data, the release, or public assurance wording, or if impact can't be determined from available context.
- Skip this process only for clearly Quick, single-item changes or when an existing `change-impact.md` already covers the exact scope.
choosing-what-to-control:
- List every file, prompt, model, dependency, tool, doc, test, or claim the change affects, then keep only items whose state affects trust, agent power, releases, repeatability, or public understanding; do not turn this into a whole-repo inventory.
- For each kept item, record its type, owner, current state, intended state, evidence link (or named gap), and a re-check trigger; name the exact target and any do-not-touch boundaries.
- Output as a controlled-item list or `controlled-items.md`; escalate to `change-impact.md` if multiple artifact kinds could go stale.
- Escalate when drift in an uncontrolled item could affect users, data, security, releases, agent power, or attribution of ideas.
- Never leave an item with no owner or re-check trigger; flag public claims or agent-power changes left uncontrolled as red flags. Do not imply formal assurance or compliance.
closing-stale-packets:
- Run `ng status .`; for every packet not tagged `ok`, determine ownership and whether the underlying change is still wanted before acting.
- Bring each stale packet to exactly one terminal state: complete it (fill prompts, pass `validate`, marker gone because filled), close it (add a `NUCLEAR-GRADE-CLOSED:` line with rationale, replacement if any, and decider), or delete it (only if genuinely empty with nothing to learn).
- Prefer closing over deleting whenever any rationale is worth preserving; never delete a placeholder marker just to fake a pass.
- Escalate to the owner before deleting any packet whose change isn't confirmed dead, and flag if changes may have shipped without proof or if abandonment is accelerating.
- Re-verify `ng status .` shows every packet as `ok` or `closed`; do not imply formal assurance, compliance, certification, or regulatory adequacy.
creating-change-records:
- Run `python tools/ng.py new <slug> --mode quick|standard`, then state by name which files that mode requires (Quick: risk.md, proof.md; Standard: risk.md, basis.md, plan.md, trace.md, verification.md, ship.md).
- Fill in only content that helps a reviewer decide; use links (affected files, tests, reviews, source-map rows, known gaps) instead of repeating information across files.
- Use plain status labels only: pass, fail, gap, deferred, not applicable, planned.
- Run `python tools/ng.py validate .nuclear/changes/<slug>`; require all links to resolve and proof/verification evidence status to be stated before calling it done.
- Escalate Quick to Standard or human review if proof can't answer the reviewer's question; stop if the record becomes a long narrative without claim-to-evidence links; never imply formal assurance or compliance.
deciding-who-decides:
- Bound the decision episode (action, policy ID/version/authority/custodian/digest, non-expired validity, reversibility) and code evidence states as observed, bounded_absence, unknown, or disputed—never treat missing telemetry as absence.
- Allocate all nine rights (prepare, recommend, verify, validate, verdict, accept, apply, reopen, close) to named actors with mandatory evidence-basis authority and required Evidence IDs; assign each an access class and derive one declaration-relative result, defaulting to policy_result_indeterminate when unclear.
- Block or transfer agent application whenever decisive evidence is unknown, disputed, self-check-only, or authority/intervention capability is unresolved; never let confidence, fluency, activity, or nominal human presence substitute for authorization.
- Record concrete transfer/reopen/blocking triggers and reopen/supersede on material changes or evidence expiry/invalidation—never silently reuse prior acceptance.
- Run `ng validate <packet> --strict-authority` (plus `--strict-custody` when needed); passing proves structural consistency only, not actual safety, security, or compliance.
declaring-intent:
- Before any critical, irreversible, or high-blast-radius action, declare "I intend to <action> on <target> because <reasoning/evidence>" and pause for review before acting.
- State the expected result plus concrete, measurable signals that would falsify it, not just success criteria.
- State numeric abort criteria and a verified (not assumed) rollback plan; confirm preconditions are proven, not assumed.
- Name who may stop the action, by when, and a backup watcher; get a second reviewer for irreversible actions if only one person has seen the reasoning.
- Stop/escalate if rollback is missing or abort criteria are unmeasurable; after acting, record actual vs. expected result and route mismatches to pause/incident. Never treat the declaration itself as approval, certification, or proof of understanding.
double-checking-before-acting:
- Before high-stakes actions (deletes, publishes, releases, migrations, public claims, trust/permission/credential changes), name the exact target, expected result, and stop condition before acting, then act only within your given authority.
- After acting, compare the real result to the expected result before claiming success; never claim success without this comparison.
- For trust-bearing actions, get an independent second check (different person or model/context), not a same-agent re-check.
- Record any mismatch, gap, or escalation in a short self-check note (action, target, expected/real result, stop condition, evidence); a mismatch halts the action rather than triggering a retry.
- Pause and escalate whenever authority, target, or evidence is unclear, or the action is unsafe/irreversible—skip this process only for tiny local edits with obvious proof or read-only actions with no downstream effect.
handing-off-work:
- Before resuming work, state last completed action, changed conditions, remaining scope, authority limits, open evidence, and stop conditions in a `turnover.md`; require the incoming owner to restate scope, authority, proof owed, and stop conditions before acting.
- Refuse to resume based on implied state or chat history alone; block action until scope and stop conditions are confirmed.
- Escalate instead of proceeding when credentials, production data, release authority, public claims, or unresolved evidence gaps are involved.
- Use this only when responsibility transfers with open work, decisions, or authority limits; do not use for finished work, quick diffs, or plain summaries.
- Flag missing last-action records, missing changed-conditions sections, mixed-in new work, or owners acting before confirming scope as failures requiring correction.
learning-from-experience:
- Treat every mistake, near miss, review surprise, or ticket as feedback showing a weak control (test, checker, rule, permission limit); fix the control, not the person, for honest errors.
- Never file a willful violation (knowingly bypassed gate, disabled control, fabricated result) as "just a mistake" — surface, correct, assign an owner, and fix the bypassable gate too.
- For each event: state actual vs. standard, find root cause and the weak control/artifact touched, then pick a lasting fix (update test, template, checker, doc, monitor, or version) rather than closing with regret alone.
- Assign an owner and verify the fix, or deliberately waive with a stated reason; escalate to a second reviewer if the same weak control recurs.
- Escalate events touching users, data, security, credentials, releases, or public claims; if a shared artifact is defective, notify downstream users in addition to fixing your own copy.
organizing-project-folders:
- Choose production-codebase or agent-workflow pattern; derive folders from a work breakdown's outline (or reverse-engineer one first), and for workflows use numbered stage folders with per-stage context files and review gates.
- For every proposed folder, check it's earned, has one reason to change, is loosely coupled, maps to exactly one work-breakdown piece or disposition rule, has a single home, and is named/documented.
- Name paths lowercase, one consistent word separator, ISO-8601 dates, single extension dot, no spaces/special chars; ban misc/utils/tmp/old/backup/final-type junk names.
- Cap nesting near 8 levels and paths near 255 characters; give each non-trivial folder a README/note stating purpose and disposition.
- Compare against existing conventions, propose minimal new structure, flag conflicts to the owner instead of overwriting; escalate if no breakdown exists or no single source of truth is reachable.
proving-claims:
- Extract every material claim; classify its support as fact, assumption, unknown, source claim, local proof, or decision authority, and never let a claim reach past its evidence.
- Assign each claim a check type (self/peer/concurrent/independent/review/test/eval) matched to depth (Quick/Standard/Nuclear), and give it a status: pass/fail/gap/deferred/not applicable/planned in trace.md or verification.md.
- For load-bearing claims, record evidence custody (who generated, selected, transformed, executed, retained, presented) and the actor–evidence coupling profile (actor, context, mechanism, authority, resource); never count a self-check as independent, and add independent reproduction or carry as residual risk if too coupled.
- Refuse to let CI results, reviewer narration, or self-authored write-ups substitute for real evidence; route produced-artifact claims to fresh observation, not generator inspection.
- Record gaps plainly for release posture; escalate/block on missing evidence, unscoped safety/security/compliance claims, or unowned fail/gap treated as shippable.
questioning-attitude:
- Restate every change as one decision question evidence could settle; name assumptions, sort into facts/assumptions/unknowns/shaky-sources, and identify the one fact that would change the decision.
- Check facts before trusting memory, confidence, or agent-generated claims; mark each assumption as checked, a gap, or assigned to someone.
- Identify applicable work type(s) (greenfield, brownfield, defect-fix, refactor-migration) and answer the questions each forces; escalate or raise rigor mode when a load-bearing assumption is a gap.
- Name concrete stop/pause/escalate conditions, get an independent reviewer if only one agent's read supports the decision, and stop when a claim lacks evidence.
- Never claim or imply formal verification, compliance, certification, safety, security, or regulatory adequacy; flag words like "probably," "safe," "approved" without evidence.
rating-change-risk:
- Before building, grade the change's stakes (consequence, reversibility, unknowns, exposure, detectability, agent power, past incidents) and select a mode: administrative floor only if purely administrative, instantly reversible, no trust boundary crossed, and no tripwire (auth, data, dependency, model/prompt, agent authority, CI, release, baseline, public claims) fires; otherwise choose at least Quick (local/easy-to-undo/easy-to-prove/no new trust boundary), Standard (user-visible, lasting, or touching dependencies/permissions/data/AI/ops/release), or a stronger human-reviewed mode (Nuclear/Incident/Research Board/Release).
- Grade the specific change, not the file it touches; take the higher of the two, and derive the grade both top-down (worst credible outcome) and bottom-up (what breaks if this edit fails).
- When unclear, raise the mode rather than lower it; escalate for money, sensitive data, security, outside trust, irreversible actions, autonomous tools, or release readiness.
- Record: mode, decision question, evidence bar, required files, proof command or gap, escalation triggers, and a suggested safety habit.
- Never claim formal verification, compliance, certification, safety, security, or regulatory adequacy.
recording-a-known-good-version:
- Record the accepted version's identity (commit/PR/release), what controlled items it includes and excludes, and link it to controlled-items.md, change-impact.md, verification.md, ship.md, and any operating lessons.
- Verify the version is exactly rebuildable from its identifying commit/PR/release, all controlled items are included or deliberately excluded, and re-check triggers are clearly documented.
- Name accepted residual gaps with owners, and record triggers that force a new baseline.
- Stop and flag as unrebuildable-baseline if evidence is missing or scope was silently dropped; escalate when the version touches customers, regulated work, safety, security, or outside-trust claims.
- Skip this when the change is trivial with nothing released, or evidence isn't ready; never imply formal assurance or compliance.
recording-what-an-agent-did:
- Record every consequential step (tool call, edit, command, API call, approval) with tool name, shortened inputs, output, and evidence status (pass/gap/fail/n-a); confirm each stayed within `basis.md` power limits.
- At decision points, log the choice made, the limit applied, and whether it was within allowed power; log token use, delay, and human approvals (reviewer, date, decision) where relevant.
- Link each trace row to a claim in `verification.md`; if a tracing platform already captures the run, link its export instead of copying it.
- Summarize scope adherence (in-scope, unclear, gaps) linked to `ship.md`; flag unevidenced-run gaps for follow-up.
- Escalate/pause on out-of-scope actions, unexpected side effects on data/credentials/production, or trace gaps blocking a release decision; run `python tools/ng.py validate` before completion.
reporting-shared-defects:
- When a defect is found in a shared/supplied artifact (prompt, skill, dependency, model, eval, template, config), evaluate downstream impact—who consumes it and how it fails for them unaware—before considering the work done.
- Treat the local fix and outward notice as separate obligations: fix your copy, but also notify affected consumers/owners with description, severity, and fix/workaround, each tied to an owner and tracking link.
- Record every case as a shared-defect report linked to the OPEX record and deficiency register; if it can't reach others, record that judgment with a reason instead of notifying.
- Escalate when the defect touches security, credentials, data integrity, privacy, or a public release, or when no one will own the notice.
- Never silently patch a shared artifact locally and move on without notifying or recording a reason.
responding-to-incidents:
- Name one incident commander, assign clear roles, and stabilize first via the safest reversible action before analyzing cause.
- Keep a running timeline labeling each entry as confirmed fact or hypothesis; never record a hypothesis as fact.
- Prefer reversible actions and block irreversible fixes until the cause is confirmed or a named owner explicitly accepts the risk; record every decision and who made it.
- Communicate status on a fixed cadence, even if unchanged, and hand off cleanly across shifts with state, open actions, and authority limits.
- Do not close the incident until stable and every corrective action has a named owner and closure trigger; then hand off to learning/deficiency records.
reviewing-code-quality:
- Read the diff against its stated goal, flag scope drift, then look for what can be deleted before rearranging anything.
- Use file/function size, deep nesting, and repeated branches as prompts to inspect closer, not hard rules; give a reason each time.
- Flag wrappers/layers that don't remove more complexity than they add, feature logic leaking into shared/core code, and clever indirection over plain code.
- Produce a ranked findings list (location, standard at risk, concrete fix) plus one unhedged verdict: VERIFIED, NOT VERIFIED, or INCONCLUSIVE, with a reason.
- Return NOT VERIFIED if findings hurt maintainability and the author disagrees; return INCONCLUSIVE naming missing context; escalate recurring drift to a control instead of another one-off review.
staying-on-mission:
- Keep a written mission anchor (goal, success criteria, non-goals) and test every action against it, not memory; restate it from the record before deciding.
- If an action serves a swapped-in smaller goal, crosses a non-goal, or loosens a standard without justification, stop and return to the anchor.
- If crossing a non-goal/standard is truly needed, escalate to the anchor's owner with a justification row (what's crossed, why, why no simpler path).
- Track retries: after 3 failed attempts at the same goal, stop retrying variants and escalate instead.
- After deciding (re-anchor/escalate/stop), update the written anchor so it survives context loss, and never imply formal compliance, certification, or safety assurance.
stress-testing-agent-changes:
- Before releasing any change that grants an agent new tools, access, or power, name its role, tools, and data reach, then select relevant attack types (prompt injection, jailbreak, extra-power gain, tool misuse, unsafe output, poisoned retrieval, data leakage, multi-turn manipulation) and run or simulate each.
- For each chosen attack type, record expected safe behavior before testing, then log the result as contained, uncertain, or exposed—never drop a finding silently.
- For every uncertain or exposed finding, document leftover risk and a backup control (power limit, filter, output check, or human approval).
- Write a before/after note and link all findings into verification.md and ship.md; run `python tools/ng.py validate .nuclear/changes/<slug>` and require it to pass.
- Escalate/pause if agent scope is unclear, if an exposed finding touches credentials/production data/users, or if formal security audit is needed; never claim "safe/secure/hardened" without attack evidence.
tracking-deficiencies:
- Log every known deficiency as a register entry with a one-line description, link to where it shows up, and first-seen date to make its age visible.
- Assign a named owner to each deficiency; treat an unowned deficiency itself as a finding.
- Give each entry a disposition: either fix by a date, or formally risk-accept it with a named owner and a concrete revisit trigger — never leave it as a silent "known issue."
- Link related incident, OPEX, and controlled-item records to each entry for traceability.
- Escalate deficiencies touching safety, security, data integrity, shared/supplied artifacts, or driving repeat incidents; don't imply formal assurance.
using-nuclear-grade:
- Before any tool call, state out loud the change's mode—administrative floor (tiny, reversible, no trust boundary crossed), Quick, or Standard-plus—plus the one fact justifying it; re-declare if scope grows.
- Force Standard-plus (never Quick) if the change touches auth/permissions/secrets, user-visible behavior, data/schema/migrations, dependencies, model/prompt/agent power, CI, or release/claim-bearing wording.
- Build the smallest fitting record: commit message only for the floor; otherwise a minimal packet under `.nuclear/changes/<slug>/` stating what it must do/prove, files touched, and claims to avoid.
- Slow down and get human review at promise boundaries: accepting claims, shipping releases, saving baselines, or changing agent permissions; run `ng.py validate` on Quick/Standard-plus records.
- Refuse to grant formal compliance/certification/safety assurance; stop and escalate if evidence, rollback, monitoring, or release decision is unclear.
verifying-final-artifacts:
- Never accept the source/code that generates an artifact as proof it's correct; always regenerate the artifact fresh and directly observe the actual output (open images, rasterize every PDF page, screenshot UI, fetch live responses) before judging it.
- Compare the observed output against the spec criterion by criterion, logging concrete defects (not "looks fine"); only then trace each defect to its responsible source line.
- Fix the source, regenerate, and re-observe from scratch each time—never assume a fix worked because the diff looks right; repeat until matching spec or a 3-loop budget is spent.
- Return INCONCLUSIVE if the real output can't be observed in this environment; escalate if the artifact is public-facing/trust-bearing and the defect would reach a consumer.
- End with one unhedged verdict (VERIFIED/NOT VERIFIED/INCONCLUSIVE), findings tied to output locations, iteration count, and no claim of formal compliance, safety, or certification.
vetting-outside-code-and-models:
- Trust any outside dependency, model, API, or SaaS only for a use as narrow as your own repo-side evidence supports; never extend trust past that.
- Name the few critical characteristics your use actually relies on, verify each yourself via a named acceptance method (test/eval, process survey, provenance check, or track record), and keep vendor/source claims strictly separate from your own verified evidence.
- Block acceptance if any critical characteristic can't be independently verified; escalate or defer instead of shipping the risk silently.
- Set a re-check trigger tied to what the acceptance rests on (version bump, model/fine-tune change, or provider process update), and document use decision, gaps, backup controls, owner, and release impact in a supplier-trust record.
- Route unresolved gaps to a ship/defer/block decision; escalate to qualified review for credentials, production data, security/privacy claims, or regulated-use fitness.
